eyebrow: Twenty measurements · one shape, one motion
h1: Flat or globe? Measure it yourself.
lead: Each card below is one thing you can do, or check, without buying anything. No explanation here on purpose: the tab behind each card carries the geometry, the sources and the numbers, and computes both models side by side. They come in two families. The first asks what shape and size the ground has; one radius, R ≈ 6,371 km, satisfies all of them at once, and no flat arrangement satisfies two. The second asks how the ground moves: it turns once in 23 h 56 min about an axis tilted to each place's vertical, and goes round the Sun once a year.
answers-lead: These eleven propose no measurement of their own, so they are set apart rather than left out: perspective, what it shrinks and what it cannot do, from receding cubes to sunbeams; refraction, which is the standard escape and is modelled everywhere on this page; surveying and levelling, which is what the profession already does about it; the observation guide, which is how to photograph a ridge without fooling yourself; the celestial theodolite, which is somebody else's experiment examined on its own terms; the atmosphere, why the air stays without a lid; rockets, what pushes a rocket in empty space and why the air only holds it back; the history of maps, which shows that the flat-earth map is itself a projection of the globe; the aether, the nineteenth-century experiments on light that flat-earth videos cite, and what they really found; the case studies, published flat-earth observations redone with their own numbers and the day's open data; and the contributions, readers' own photographs measured against both models.
collab-lead: One point cannot reveal a sphere: its radius needs positions far apart. These modules are neither demonstrations nor tools. Each person measures alone, in their own browser, and the site stores and sends nothing; then people thousands of kilometres apart exchange their results by hand and check that they find the same radius.
falsify-link: The last tab, “What would refute each model”, collects the mirror of every card: the result that would refute each model, stated in advance.
do-elev: Photograph a distant peak and measure how high it sits above the horizon.
do-hh: Watch a ship leave: the hull goes before the mast, and always in that order.
do-cnav: Measure the altitude of Polaris from two cities and subtract.
do-star: Photograph the star trails for an hour. Note which way they turn.
do-dist: Time a long-haul flight and compare it with the distance your map claims.
do-dip: From a cliff, measure how far below eye level the sea horizon sits.
do-curv: From an aircraft window, measure how much the horizon bends in a photo — and see why it looks flat from the beach.
do-grav: Weigh the same object at the equator and near a pole.
do-fou: Hang a long pendulum and mark where it swings every hour.
do-seis: Take one earthquake and read its arrival times at two distant stations.
do-mag: Let a compass needle tilt freely on a horizontal axis and read the angle.
do-sun: Measure the Sun's angular width in January and again in July.
do-twi: Time how long the sky stays lit after the Sun has gone down.
do-azim: Point at the Sun and read the compass bearing, then look up the place beneath it.
do-gps: Open your phone's GPS status screen and watch satellites rise and set.
do-rx: Record your phone's raw satellite signals, solve your own position, then measure the Earth's radius with people far away.
do-avia: Time a long-haul flight in the southern hemisphere, both ways — or watch a heading gyro drift.
do-ref: Where R/(1 − k) comes from, and why one coefficient has to serve every tab.
do-surv: Two centuries of professional procedure that exist only because flat arithmetic kept missing.
do-obs: How to photograph a ridge against the Sun without fooling yourself — and this page's own attempt.
do-ct: Somebody else's experiment, taken seriously: a clock instead of a theodolite.
do-ecl: Look up the published path of the 2 August 2027 eclipse, then check the time and the duration where you stand.
do-rot: Read the Earth's rotation from ring lasers and falling balls, and see why the latitude dependence rules out both flat models.
do-orb: Size the Earth's orbit from aberration, light time and the Doppler shift of the Sun and of τ Ceti.
do-moon: The Earth's radius from laser pulses fired at the Moon from Grasse, and two Moon measurements to make yourself.
geo-h2: Geometry: the shape and the size
geo-lead: Angles, distances, times and gravity measured at different places, each read against both models. None of these needs the Earth to move.
mov-h2: Motions: the rotation and the orbit
mov-lead: Instruments that feel the Earth turn, and light that shows it moving through the year. A plane at rest predicts none of it; a disc spinning about its pole predicts the same rotation everywhere.
both-lead: These tabs use the rotation or the orbit to test the shape, or the reverse: the Sun's daily and yearly path, the stars turning about the pole, a pendulum's slow turn, airliners and their gyroscopes.
do-results: The Earth's radius measured some fifteen ways, the rotation and the orbit: every result of the site on one page, measurements and checks kept apart.
do-map: From a Babylonian clay disc to Ptolemy, Mercator and Gauss: why small maps are flat, why the world map cannot be, and where the flat-earth map comes from.
do-contrib: Readers' photographs measured with open data: a tower 13 km away across Gulf St Vincent, hidden by the sea, and what each model needs from the air to hide it.
do-sat: Fit 79 satellites' orbits, 80 receivers, the Earth's mass and rotation to one day of Doppler, starting from a flat map.
do-scale: See the Earth's motions on one clock, each hand at its true speed, and the distances from the Moon to Andromeda.
do-atmo: Why the air stays without a lid, how the ionosphere bends radio waves, and why satellites do not melt in a thousand-degree thermosphere.
do-aether: Airy's water telescope, Michelson–Morley, Sagnac, Michelson–Gale: what the aether was, what each experiment measured, and how special relativity came out of it.
do-phys: Units, derivatives and their notations, frames of reference, Newton's laws, the constants and uncertainties: the definitions every other tab relies on, each with its formula and a figure.
do-rocket: Molecules hitting walls: why a closed chamber goes nowhere, how a fire keeps its pressure, and why a rocket pushes harder in a vacuum than in air.
do-cases: A laser seen across 15 km of sea, redone with the operators' own thermometers and that evening's air, sea and tide: what it takes to see it, and what their readings could tell.
hreel-alt: Animated showcase of the site's approach: a globe and a flat disc on one balance; a table of verdicts written in advance; bars counting the sections that are measures, checks and model predictions; a flat model's free parameter swept to its best case, still short of the data; the counts of tabs, sources, datasets and verdicts; a terminal rebuilding each dataset; the Earth's radius from measurements alone; and the question of what would change our mind
hreel-cap: The site in fifty seconds: its rules rather than its results. Every number in it is counted from the site itself (tabs, sources, datasets, badged sections, the radius from measurements alone); the drawings are schematic. Click the animation to pause it.
hreel-schem: schematic; every number counted from the site
hreel-intro-a: Two models, the same experiments, the same rules.
hreel-intro-b: This site puts both to the test, and says beforehand what would prove each one right.
hreel-advance-a: Every experiment first states what result would vindicate the flat model.
hreel-advance-b: Then the data decide. The verdicts have a tab of their own.
hreel-classes-a: A measure: the radius never entered its data. A check: real data compared with the globe.
hreel-classes-b: A model: a prediction, nothing measured. Every section says which it is.
hreel-cls-measure-d: the radius never entered the data
hreel-cls-unit: sections of the site, by class
hreel-steel-k: The flat model at its best
hreel-steel-a: Where the flat model has a free parameter, it is tuned in its favour.
hreel-steel-b: It still misses. And each method's own limits are written in the text.
hreel-steel-x: the flat model's free parameter (its Sun's height…)
hreel-counts-a: Every claim carries a numbered source.
hreel-counts-b: Every figure comes from data anyone can download.
hreel-redo-a: The raw files, the code and every step are public.
hreel-redo-b: One command rebuilds each dataset from its raw files.
hreel-radius-a: Methods whose data the Earth's radius never entered…
hreel-radius-b: …agree on one sphere. A flat Earth has no radius to find.
hreel-rad-flat: on a plane: no radius at all
hreel-outro-b: Each tab says it, in advance. Look, measure, check.
do-persp: Four cubes moving away, a Sun that cannot set by perspective, sunbeams that fan out and close up again: what perspective shrinks, and what it cannot hide.
do-rules: Fixed before the results: no silent exaggeration, the flat model at its best, the globe never fitted to our data, the same margins for both, refraction always shown, what is set aside and why. The rules every tab follows.
